```{python}
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

import duckdb
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Markdown, display

from user_journey.model import STATE_NAMES, forecast, state_counts, transition_matrix, with_active_totals
from user_journey.states import DAU_DATA, states

plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")

# figures are saved next to the post; the article editor swaps each for its own link when it is uploaded
ASSETS = Path("assets")
ASSETS.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
shutil.copy("states.png", ASSETS / "states.png")  # the hand-drawn state diagram


def figure(fig, name, alt):
    fig.savefig(ASSETS / f"{name}.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)
    display(Markdown(f"![{alt}]({ASSETS}/{name}.png)"))


def num(x, digits=0):
    return f"{x:,.{digits}f}"


def pct(x, digits=1):
    return f"{100 * x:+.{digits}f}%"


dau_data = pd.read_csv(DAU_DATA, parse_dates=["date", "registration_date"])

con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute("SET enable_progress_bar = false")  # keep DuckDB's progress bars out of the post
user_states = states(con)
actual = with_active_totals(state_counts(user_states))

# training: the transition matrix is estimated on the year before the test period
# test: the last six months of data; the chain starts from the state counts on the last training day
TRAIN_START, TRAIN_END = "2022-05-01", "2023-04-30"
TEST_START, TEST_END = "2023-05-01", "2023-10-31"

m = transition_matrix(user_states, TRAIN_START, TRAIN_END)
m_test = transition_matrix(user_states, TEST_START, TEST_END)
state0 = actual.loc[TRAIN_END, STATE_NAMES]
test = actual.loc[TEST_START:TEST_END]
predicted = forecast(m, state0, test["new"])  # actual new users each day, from outside the chain
error = (predicted - test) / test  # relative error per day
# the same test with the matrix estimated on the test period itself: what is left is not drift
oracle = forecast(m_test, state0, test["new"])
oracle_error = (oracle - test) / test
monthly_abs = abs(error[["dau", "wau", "mau"]].groupby(error.index.to_period("M")).mean())
```

# How Well Does a Markov Chain Predict Active Users?

## Testing a Duolingo-Style Model of User States on Six Months of Held-Out Data

Duolingo [described](https://blog.duolingo.com/growth-model-duolingo) a simple way to think about active users: every user is in one of a handful of states each day (new, current, at risk, dormant, ...), users move between states with stable probabilities, and daily, weekly and monthly active users are just sums over states. The probabilities form a transition matrix, and pushing today's state counts through it says where the user base is heading.

This post builds that model from the activity logs of a simulated app and tests the part that is about user behaviour: **the transitions**. The transition matrix is estimated on a year of data, and then used to predict the last six months, which the model never saw. New users are not part of the test: they come from outside the chain, so the actual number of sign-ups each day is fed in. Any error is then down to how users move between states. Everything is open:

- 🎮 **Try it:** [Space: user-journey-what-if](https://huggingface.co/spaces/prteek/user-journey-what-if): replay the test months with different retention and see what happens to active users
- 📊 **Data:** [datasets/prteek/user-journey-dau](https://huggingface.co/datasets/prteek/user-journey-dau): the activity records
- 💻 **Code:** [github.com/prteek/probabilistic-model-of-user-journey](https://github.com/prteek/probabilistic-model-of-user-journey)

## TL;DR

- Give every user one of **seven states** each day, estimate the **transition matrix** between states from a year of history, and push the state counts through it day by day, adding each day's new users.
- Tested on six held-out months, the chain predicts weekly active users within `{python} f"{abs(error['wau']).mean():.1%}"` on average and daily active users within `{python} f"{abs(error['dau']).mean():.1%}"`, with the error growing over time: in the last month DAU is `{python} pct(-error.loc['2023-10', 'dau'].mean(), 0).lstrip('+')` too low and MAU `{python} pct(error.loc['2023-10', 'mau'].mean(), 0).lstrip('+')` too high.
- The drift has a clear cause: users stayed more engaged in the test period than in the training year. Next-day retention of new users went from `{python} f"{m.loc['new', 'current']:.0%}"` to `{python} f"{m_test.loc['new', 'current']:.0%}"`. A fixed transition matrix can't see that; comparing matrices over time can.

## User states

On each day of a user's life, they are in exactly one of seven states:

- **new**: using the app for the first time
- **current**: active today, and also active in the past week
- **reactivated**: active today, last active in the past month but not the past week
- **resurrected**: active today, last active more than 30 days ago
- **at_risk_wau**: not active today, but active in the past week
- **at_risk_mau**: active in the past month, but not the past week
- **dormant**: inactive for more than 30 days

![User states and the transitions between them](assets/states.png)

The arrows are the quantities a product team watches: the share of new users who come back the next day, the share of current users who stay current, the share of at-risk users who return, and so on.

## The model

Let $M$ be the transition matrix: $m_{ij}$ is the probability that a user in state $i$ today is in state $j$ tomorrow, and each row sums to 1. If $u_t$ holds the expected number of users in each state on day $t$, then, assuming the transition probabilities don't change over time,

$$
u_{t+1} = M^\top u_t ,
$$

except that new users don't come from any state: they join from outside the chain, so the number of new users on each day is an input. Daily, weekly and monthly active users are sums over states:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{DAU}_t &= \#\text{new}_t + \#\text{current}_t + \#\text{reactivated}_t + \#\text{resurrected}_t \\
\text{WAU}_t &= \text{DAU}_t + \#\text{at\_risk\_wau}_t \\
\text{MAU}_t &= \text{WAU}_t + \#\text{at\_risk\_mau}_t
\end{aligned}
$$

## The data

The data is a simulated activity log based on a real SaaS app: one row per user per day they were active, with the user's registration date.

```{python}
display(Markdown(dau_data.head(5).assign(
    date=lambda d: d["date"].dt.date, registration_date=lambda d: d["registration_date"].dt.date
).to_markdown(index=False)))
```

It covers `{python} num(dau_data['user_id'].nunique())` users from `{python} f"{dau_data['date'].min():%-d %B %Y}"` to `{python} f"{dau_data['date'].max():%-d %B %Y}"`, `{python} num(len(dau_data))` active user-days in all. The transition matrix is estimated on the year from `{python} f"{pd.Timestamp(TRAIN_START):%-d %B %Y}"` to `{python} f"{pd.Timestamp(TRAIN_END):%-d %B %Y}"`, and the last six months are held out for testing:

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.6))
ax.plot(actual.index, actual["dau"], color="black", lw=0.8)
ax.axvspan(pd.Timestamp(TRAIN_START), pd.Timestamp(TRAIN_END), color="tab:blue", alpha=0.08, label="training year")
ax.axvspan(pd.Timestamp(TEST_START), pd.Timestamp(TEST_END), color="tab:red", alpha=0.08, label="test (held out)")
ax.set_ylabel("daily active users")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left")
figure(fig, "dau", "Daily active users, with the training year and the held-out test period")
```

## From activity records to states

The activity log only lists days when a user was active. To assign states, every user needs a row for **every** day from their first active day to the end of the data, marked active or not; each day's state then follows from whether the user was active and how long ago they were last active. That is `{python} num(user_states.count('*').fetchall()[0][0])` user-days, which DuckDB builds from the activity log in a few seconds with a window function:

```sql
max(case when is_active then date end) over (
    partition by user_id order by date rows between unbounded preceding and 1 preceding
) as last_active
```

Here is one user over two weeks, going quiet, slipping from *current* to *at risk*, and coming back:

```{python}
example = (
    user_states.filter("user_id like '269b7f13-a509-5174-85cb%' and date between '2020-10-18' and '2020-10-30'")
    .order("date").df()
    .assign(
        user_id=lambda d: d["user_id"].str[:8] + "…",
        date=lambda d: d["date"].dt.date,
        registration_date=lambda d: d["registration_date"].dt.date,
    )
)
display(Markdown(example.to_markdown(index=False)))
```

## The transition matrix

The transition matrix is estimated by counting, over the training year, how often users move from each state to each other state from one day to the next, and dividing by the number of moves out of each state:

```sql
select state as state_from, lead(state) over (partition by user_id order by date) as state_to
from states
```

```{python}
display(Markdown(m.rename_axis("today ↓ / tomorrow →").to_markdown(floatfmt=".4f")))
```

It reads sensibly:

- **Current users mostly stay current.** `{python} f"{m.loc['current', 'current']:.1%}"` are active again the next day; the rest become *at risk*.
- **New users are fragile.** Only `{python} f"{m.loc['new', 'current']:.1%}"` are active on their second day.
- **Nobody becomes new.** The *new* column is all zeros: new users only enter from outside the chain.
- **Dormant users rarely return.** `{python} f"{m.loc['dormant', 'dormant']:.2%}"` of dormant users are still dormant the next day. On the last training day, `{python} num(state0['dormant'])` of the `{python} num(state0.sum())` users are dormant, so even a small improvement there would be worth a resurrection campaign.

## Testing on six held-out months

The test starts from the actual state counts on `{python} f"{pd.Timestamp(TRAIN_END):%-d %B %Y}"`, the last training day. Each day moves the previous day's expected counts through $M$ and adds that day's actual new users:

```python
for n_new in new_users:
    u = M.T @ u
    u[STATE_NAMES.index("new")] = n_new
```

Feeding in the actual new users keeps the test about transitions. Almost everyone who joins the chain in the test period does so as a new user; the actual state counts, computed from the states table, are the benchmark.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.6))
history = actual.loc["2023-02-01":TRAIN_END]
for ax, col, label in zip(axes, ["dau", "wau", "mau"], ["daily", "weekly", "monthly"]):
    ax.plot(history.index, history[col], color="0.6", lw=0.8, label="training data")
    ax.plot(test.index, test[col], color="black", lw=0.8, label="actual")
    ax.plot(predicted.index, predicted[col], color="tab:red", lw=1.5, label="predicted")
    ax.axvline(pd.Timestamp(TEST_START), color="0.4", lw=0.8, ls=":")
    ax.set_title(f"{label} active users", fontsize=10)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=30, labelsize=8)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower left")
figure(fig, "test", "Daily, weekly and monthly active users in the test period: actual and predicted")
```

```{python}
monthly = error[["dau", "wau", "mau"]].groupby(error.index.to_period("M")).mean()
monthly.index = [f"{p:%b %Y}" for p in monthly.index]
table = monthly.map(pct).rename(columns={"dau": "DAU", "wau": "WAU", "mau": "MAU"})
table.loc["all six months (mean absolute)"] = abs(error[["dau", "wau", "mau"]]).mean().map(lambda x: f"{100 * x:.1f}%").values
display(Markdown(table.rename_axis("mean error, predicted vs actual").to_markdown(colalign=["left", "right", "right", "right"])))
```

For a model with seven states and no knowledge of the calendar, this does well at first. In the first month every measure is within `{python} f"{monthly_abs.iloc[0].max():.0%}"`, and weekly active users stay within `{python} f"{monthly_abs['wau'].max():.0%}"` in every month. The chain reproduces little of DAU's weekday swing (it tracks expected counts, and its small wiggles come from the daily new users fed in), but it follows the level.

The errors do grow, though, and in a consistent direction: DAU drifts low and MAU drifts high. The chain moves too many users out of activity and into the *at risk* states. By the last day of the test:

```{python}
end = pd.DataFrame({"actual": test.iloc[-1][STATE_NAMES], "predicted": predicted.iloc[-1][STATE_NAMES]})
end["difference"] = end["predicted"] - end["actual"]
display(Markdown(end.rename_axis("state on " + f"{pd.Timestamp(TEST_END):%-d %B %Y}").to_markdown(floatfmt=",.0f")))
```

## What changed: comparing transition matrices

The model's one assumption is that the transition matrix doesn't change. Estimating it again on the test period shows whether that held:

```{python}
pairs = [
    ("new", "current"), ("current", "current"), ("at_risk_wau", "current"),
    ("reactivated", "current"), ("at_risk_mau", "reactivated"), ("at_risk_mau", "dormant"),
]
drift = pd.DataFrame(
    [(f"{a} → {b}", m.loc[a, b], m_test.loc[a, b]) for a, b in pairs],
    columns=["transition", "training year", "test period"],
)
drift["change"] = (drift["test period"] - drift["training year"]).map(lambda x: f"{100 * x:+.2f} pp")
display(Markdown(drift.to_markdown(index=False, floatfmt=".2%")))
```

It didn't, quite. Users were more engaged in the test period than in the training year, most of all new users: `{python} f"{m_test.loc['new', 'current']:.0%}"` came back on their second day, against `{python} f"{m.loc['new', 'current']:.0%}"` before. At-risk users also returned more often. Each change is a point or less on most transitions, but they compound every day, and over six months they add up to the drift above. A product change, a seasonal effect or a different mix of new users could all be behind it; the matrix doesn't say which, only where to look.

To check that the drift explains the errors, the test can be re-run with the matrix estimated on the test period itself, as if the change had been known in advance. The mean absolute error of MAU falls from `{python} f"{abs(error['mau']).mean():.1%}"` to `{python} f"{abs(oracle_error['mau']).mean():.1%}"`, and the surplus of *at_risk_mau* users on the last day from `{python} num(predicted.iloc[-1]['at_risk_mau'] - test.iloc[-1]['at_risk_mau'])` to `{python} num(oracle.iloc[-1]['at_risk_mau'] - test.iloc[-1]['at_risk_mau'])`. What is left is the model's own limits. DAU stays around `{python} f"{abs(oracle_error['dau']).mean():.0%}"` off on a typical day, because the chain predicts a smooth expected level and real DAU swings with the day of the week. And the chain is memoryless: a real user goes dormant after exactly 30 inactive days, while the chain gives every *at_risk_mau* user the same small chance of going dormant each day, whatever their history.

## Lessons learned

- **Test the transitions on their own.** Feeding in the actual new users separates the two things a user forecast depends on: how many people join, and how they behave once they have. Here the behaviour part predicts weekly active users within `{python} f"{abs(error['wau']).mean():.1%}"` on average over six months.
- **States make retention concrete.** A transition matrix turns vague questions ("are we keeping users?") into specific rates a team can measure and target: next-day retention of new users, of current users, of users at risk.
- **Drift shows up in the matrix before it shows up in the totals.** Comparing transition matrices over time pins a forecast error on specific transitions. Here, better retention, of new users above all, explains most of it: with the test period's own matrix, the MAU error falls from `{python} f"{abs(error['mau']).mean():.1%}"` to `{python} f"{abs(oracle_error['mau']).mean():.1%}"`.
- **Re-estimate regularly.** A matrix estimated on rolling windows tracks changes in behaviour; one fixed for six months slowly falls behind.
- **Campaigns are edits to the matrix.** A reminder that brings back some *at-risk* users raises the at-risk → current probability; a resurrection campaign raises dormant → resurrected. Re-running the chain with the edited matrix shows the effect on active users.
- **Let the database do the expansion.** Turning activity logs into one row per user per day is the expensive step. A window function in DuckDB does it in seconds, where row-by-row code in memory struggles.

## Reproduce it

The [dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/prteek/user-journey-dau) has the activity records (`dau_data.csv`); the states are rebuilt from them in seconds. The code above lives in the `user_journey` package in the [repository](https://github.com/prteek/probabilistic-model-of-user-journey):

```python
import duckdb
from user_journey.model import forecast, state_counts, transition_matrix, with_active_totals
from user_journey.states import states

s = states(duckdb.connect())
actual = with_active_totals(state_counts(s))
m = transition_matrix(s, "2022-05-01", "2023-04-30")
test = actual.loc["2023-05-01":]
predicted = forecast(m, actual.loc["2023-04-30", m.index], test["new"])
```

Or open the [Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/prteek/user-journey-what-if): it replays the six test months with the sliders on the transitions a product team can act on, such as at-risk → current, and shows what that would have done to DAU, WAU and MAU next to what really happened.
